question: How many languages were there before the Tower of Babel was built?
summary: Genesis 11:1 declares that 'the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech' before God confounds speech at Babel. Genesis 10:5, 20, 31 — one chapter earlier — already describes the descendants of Noah as divided 'every one after his tongue' in multiple languages.

reconcile.connective: Defenders read Genesis 10 as proleptic: its language-divided nations describe the outcome of the Babel confusion that chapter 11 only narrates afterward.

discrepancy.connective: Steven DiMattei presses the conflict as a seam between sources, arguing the Priestly table of nations (Gen 10) treats distinct languages as a natural genealogical given, while the Yahwist Babel story (Gen 11) makes one original tongue divinely confused only later.

skeptic.name: Steven DiMattei
skeptic.attribution: Steven DiMattei, Contradictions in the Bible, no. 22, "One Language From Many, or Many From One?" (2013)

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Genesis 10:5
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill harmonizes this exact pair, holding that the division of nations in Gen 10 'is by way of anticipation; and that, though thus related, was not done till after the confusion of languages' at Babel in Gen 11.

link.title: CARM: Does Genesis contradict itself regarding when human languages divided?

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Every one after his tongue - This refers to the time posterior to the confusion of tongues and dispersion from Babel.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the tension: it reads Gen 10:5's 'every one after his tongue' as describing a time AFTER the Babel confusion of ch. 11, i.e. ch. 10 is proleptic, so the 'many languages before one language' ordering is only apparent.
